tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

A workflow size guideline is configured for this session: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale.

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. ## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

content.text:
**Something went wrong during the check.** To time indexing, the agent ran `memsearch index` twice against an empty temp folder. That command isn't read-only: it compares the index with the folders you give it and deletes everything not in them. About **12,900 of ~31,000 vectors were deleted**, roughly 40% of the index, before the runs stopped. Your memory files on disk are untouched; only the search index lost entries. The fix is to rebuild the index, which takes a few hours (details under "What I recommend" below).

**What's actually been failing (two separate problems):**

1. **10/06, "Milvus unreachable":** Docker Desktop's port forward to Milvus kept dropping and coming back: 120 times on 10/05 and 176 times on 10/06. Each drop matches a memsearch failure to the second. Milvus itself never restarted. This seems to build up when Docker runs for days through repeated laptop sleeps (3.3 days of uptime here). Your reboot and the Docker restart today cleared it: zero drops so far on 10/07. The underlying cause is still unknown.
2. **10/07, `ETIMEDOUT` ×9:** Milvus was healthy and indexing wasn't hung, just slow, at about 1.2 seconds per chunk. The laptop had only 0.9–2 GB of free RAM out of 15.6 GB. Four Claude sessions, WSL, Defender and the 2.5 GB embedding model were all competing for memory. The hook's 600-second limit killed each run partway through, after about 965 rows had been written.
   - The failure streak keeps climbing because `KeystoneOS-DailyBackup` has been **disabled since 8/13**. That job did the nightly full reindex and reset the streak. On Windows, the end-of-session hook is now the only thing that indexes.
   - The index already had gaps before the deletion (for example, 133 of 293 meeting notes were missing).

**How your old memory notes hold up:**
- **timeout-cap:** the mechanism is right, but the nightly reindex and streak reset it relies on don't exist on Windows, and its timing figures came from the Mac.
- **milvus-lock-misdiagnosis:** applies only to the Mac.
- **index-path-drift:** fixed; all 13 paths resolve.
- **git-bash-stall:** not involved.

Google Drive changing file timestamps does **not** cause re-embedding; only renames do.

**What I recommend, in order:**
1. **Rebuild the index now** with one `memsearch index` run over **all 13 paths**. It takes hours, and it goes faster with fewer Claude sessions open. The exact path list matters: leave one out and that part of the index gets wiped too. I'd take the list straight from the hook's config.
2. **Change the hook** so it doesn't kill a run that's still making progress at 600 seconds, and track the two failure types separately. No admin rights needed.
3. **Re-enable a nightly full reindex on Windows,** or remove the hook's reliance on one.
4. **Free up memory,** possibly by lowering the WSL limit in `.wslconfig`. That needs a Docker restart.
5. **If the port forward starts dropping again** after long sleep periods, restart Docker Desktop.

Should I start the rebuild (step 1) in the background now? I'd also save a memory note that `memsearch index` deletes anything outside the paths it's given, so this doesn't happen again.

result: The memsearch failures have two causes: Docker's port forward kept dropping on 10/06 (cleared by today's reboot), and on 10/07 low RAM made indexing too slow for the hook's 600-second limit. The investigation also deleted ~40% of the index, which a multi-hour rebuild will fix.

1	#!/usr/bin/env node
2	// SessionEnd hook: re-index memsearch so transcripts written this session
3	// become searchable.
4	//
5	// Runs the index in a DETACHED BACKGROUND WORKER (see the self-respawn block
6	// below). The hook process returns in milliseconds; the worker outlives it and
7	// indexes at its own pace.
8	//
9	// This replaced a synchronous spawnSync capped at 45s, changed 2026-09-02.
10	// The old design assumed a ~17s fixed floor and a "~5s incremental" — numbers
11	// that were true when they were written and are not any more. Measured on this
12	// Mac 2026-09-02 against the current corpus (10 paths, ~1,450 files, of which
13	// SecondBrain/Inbox/meetings is 593 and SecondBrain/Knowledge is 334):
14	//   * no-op run, nothing new to embed ....... 33s   (was ~17s)
15	//   * one day of accumulated content ....... 278s   (232 chunks, ~1s/chunk)
16	// So the 45s cap left ~12s of embedding budget — under a dozen new chunks.
17	// Every ordinary session-end index was timing out, and incremental indexing had
18	// quietly degraded to "whatever the 09:00 nightly full reindex picks up",
19	// leaving search up to 24h stale. The tell was six session-ends inside 47
20	// minutes on 2026-09-01 producing a 7-long ETIMEDOUT streak. Raising the cap
21	// was not an option: a correct cap is minutes, and a SessionEnd hook may not
22	// block session teardown for minutes.
23	//
24	// The original rationale for staying synchronous was a WINDOWS process-group
25	// race — a detached child got killed when the parent hard-exited before its
26	// group was established. **That rationale is dead.** This machine has been
27	// macOS since 2026-08-05, where detached + unref is reliable. Do not "restore"
28	// the synchronous version on the strength of that comment.
29	//
30	// The worker keeps the full original body: it owns the PID lock (so clustered
31	// session-ends still elect a single indexer), writes INDEX_LOG, and runs every
32	// error-classification branch. Its spawnSync cap is now 600s — no longer a
33	// budget, just a runaway guard, so an ETIMEDOUT genuinely means ">10 minutes"
34	// and is worth escalating. See project_memsearch_setup.md.

content.content:
# memsearch-drain.ps1 -- one-off foreground catch-up of the memsearch backlog.
#
# Why (2026-09-28, Windows laptop): ~10,100 chunks were never indexed. The
# SessionEnd hook caps each run at 600s and this CPU embeds ~5 s/chunk with
# bge-m3, so every run was killed after ~110 chunks and the next session end
# restarted it -- 2.5-3 GB of RAM all day. This runs the same incremental
# index with no cap, once, then gets out of the way.
#
# Coordination: holds ~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.memsearch-index.lock
# with THIS process's PID for the whole run (the hook skips while the owner is
# alive), and refreshes .memsearch-last-run so the hook's 30-min cooldown is in
# force when it finishes. Runs BelowNormal so interactive work keeps the CPU.
# batch_size comes from ~/.memsearch/config.toml (8 since 2026-09-28).

$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
$T       = Join-Path $env:USERPROFILE '.claude\global-memory\transcripts'
$lock    = Join-Path $T '.memsearch-index.lock'
$lastRun = Join-Path $T '.memsearch-last-run'
$streak  = Join-Path $T '.memsearch-timeout-streak'

Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\memory-write

# Memory Write

## Outcome
- Fact added to, updated in, or removed from the correct memory tier
- Tier-B caps enforced (2,500 chars for MEMORY.md, 1,375 for USER.md)
- Confirmation: "Saved — will be active from next session."

## Pick the tier first

Ask: "Will this fact still be true and useful in 3 months, across multiple projects?"

**Tier A — `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`** (one file per fact, indexed by MEMORY.md)
- Durable user facts → `user_*.md` (metadata.type: user)
- Stable project conventions / gotchas → `project_*.md` (metadata.type: project)
- Behavioral feedback rules → `feedback_*.md` (metadata.type: feedback)
- External-system pointers → `reference_*.md` (metadata.type: reference)

**Tier B — `~/.claude/global-memory/`** (single capped file)
- Active threads (in-progress work) → `MEMORY.md` `## Active Threads`
- Current env notes (URLs, tool versions, project structure in play) → `MEMORY.md` `## Environment Notes`
- Pending decisions → `MEMORY.md` `## Pending Decisions`
- Durable user profile updates → `USER.md`

## Steps

1. **Decide tier** using the rule above.
2. **Read** the target file in full.
3. **Dedup check** — substring scan; if the fact already exists, skip or update in place.
4. **Cap check** for Tier B — `wc -c < ~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` (or USER.md). If over cap, consolidate (merge similar entries, prune stale) before adding.
5. **Write** the change.
   - Tier A: create a new file with proper frontmatter (name, description, metadata.type) and add a one-line pointer to that slug's `MEMORY.md` index. `name:` follows the rule below.
   - Tier B: append under the correct `##` section.
6. **Confirm** in one line: `Saved — will be active from next session.`

## The `name:` field — bare kebab slug

**`name:` = the filename stem minus its leading type token, kebab-cased.** The type
already lives in `metadata.type` and the filename already carries the prefix; repeating
it in `name:` is the third copy.

| File | `name:` |
|---|---|
| `project_automation-cadence.md` | `automation-cadence` |
| `user_sports-teams.md` | `sports-teams` |
| `reference_baylor-house-style.md` | `baylor-house-style` |
| `feedback_project_idea_capture.md` | `project-idea-capture` |

Note the last row: strip only the **leading** token. `feedback_project_idea_capture.md`
is a feedback memory *about* project-idea capture — its name keeps the word `project`.

`[[links]]` target this bare name, never the filename and never a prefixed variant.

This rule exists because it was previously unwritten: an audit on 2026-09-02 found the
corpus split 59 bare / 58 prefixed, which broke 37 links. Both forms look right in
isolation, so without a stated rule the split regrows on every write.

## Actions

- **add** — append (default)
- **replace** — substring match + swap. Preferred over add when updating an existing fact.
- **remove** — confirm with the user before deleting.

## Retrieval — the tiered ladder

When the user asks about past context, decisions, or "did we already…?", climb in order and stop as soon as the question is answered. Do not run memsearch when the answer is already in the injected snapshot.

1. **Tier 0** — scan what is already in context (USER.md, MEMORY.md, today's compiled log). Zero cost.
2. **L1** — `memsearch search "query" --top-k 5`. Hybrid vector + keyword across all indexed paths: Tier A files (including the Windows-machine slugs), daily logs, transcripts.
3. **L2** — `memsearch expand <chunk_hash>`. Full markdown section around a hit.
4. **L3** — `memsearch transcript <session_id>`. Raw dialogue. Last resort.
5. **Fallback** — say "I don't have a record of that."

## Daily compiled logs — read-only

`~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/daily/{YYYY-MM-DD}.md` is produced by `claude-memory-compiler` through its own SessionEnd/PreCompact hooks, and injected by its own SessionStart hook.

- **Never hand-edit these files.** The compiler owns them.
- **Never read them eagerly.** Treat the injected snapshot as the source of truth.

## What is loaded at session start

`~/.claude/global-memory/USER.md` and `MEMORY.md` are read once at session start and are a **frozen snapshot**. Mid-session writes persist to disk but only take effect next session — this is deliberate, to preserve the prefix cache. Never load more than the startup set proactively.

## Rules

- Never exceed Tier B caps. Consolidate first.
- Always dedup before adding.
- For Tier A, the slug is the current cwd with `/` and `.` replaced by `-` (so `~` → `-Users-kristinarash`, `~/DEV` → `-Users-kristinarash-DEV`, `~/.claude/skills` → `-Users-kristinarash--claude-skills`). The harness injects the correct slug each session — use that, don't reconstruct it.
- **Write only to the current machine's slug.** Both machines are active as of 2026-09-10: Mac slugs are `-Users-kristinarash-*`, Windows slugs are `C--Users-eric-rash-*`. A fact written to the other machine's slug is never auto-injected here (memsearch still finds it). Durable project facts belong in the repo's `docs/` so both machines see them.
- Never announce the write mid-session beyond the one-line confirmation. The injected snapshot is frozen — the new fact appears next session, not this one.

## Verification Gate

After every write:

1. Read the exact destination back and require the intended fact to appear once in the intended tier.
2. Re-run the Tier B character cap check after the write.
3. Check the surrounding section for an unresolved contradiction or stale duplicate. Resolve it or report `FAIL`.
4. For Tier A, verify the new file has valid frontmatter and the memory index pointer resolves to it.
5. Distinguish persisted state from activation: the write can pass now, but next-session injection remains unverified until a later session observes it.

Report `PASS` only when persistence, uniqueness, tier placement, caps, and pointers are verified. Report `FAIL` with the target path and failed check otherwise. Do not emit “Saved” before read-back succeeds.

---
name: memsearch-index-is-destructive
description: "`memsearch index <paths>` deletes every indexed source outside the given paths — never run it with a partial or test path set; plus the 2026-10-07 Windows failure causes"
metadata:
  type: project
---

`memsearch index <paths>` is **never read-only**. It reconciles the collection against
the path set it is given and deletes every indexed source not under those paths
(core.py `index()` → store.py delete). An empty or partial path set wipes the rest.

On 2026-10-07 a diagnostic run against an empty temp dir deleted ~12,900 of ~31,000
vectors before it was stopped. Recovery: a full re-index over all 13 paths in
